pests.name: Onion thrips
pests.identification_seasoned: Tiny slender insects rasping silvery streaks and flecks into the leaf necks and folds; heavy feeding reduces clump size and invites disease.
pests.identification_beginner: Very small insects that leave silvery streaks and specks on the leaves, often down in the crease where leaves meet. Bad infestations shrink the bulbs.
pests.cause_seasoned: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) build through warm, dry spells, sheltering in the leaf axils where sprays miss them.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny insect called onion thrips. It multiplies fast in warm, dry weather and hides in the tight folds of the leaves.
pests.management_seasoned: Rogue out volunteer alliums and clear crop debris at season's end, since thrips overwinter in allium material left on the surface, and site shallots away from small grains, alfalfa or clover, which shed thrips into alliums when they dry down or are cut. Keep nitrogen adequate rather than heavy, since excess promotes thrips, and water well: vigor buys tolerance of the feeding, not fewer thrips. A hard spray of water into the leaf folds knocks a light infestation back, straw mulch on the bed deters thrips, and minute pirate bugs and lacewings help where broad-spectrum sprays are avoided. Treat persistent outbreaks per local extension guidance.
pests.management_beginner: Pull any onion-family plants left in the bed at the end of the season and clear the debris, because that is where thrips spend the winter, and keep shallots away from a grain, alfalfa or clover patch, which sends thrips into them when it dries or is cut. Go easy on nitrogen, which makes thrips worse, and keep the plants well watered so they can shrug off the feeding. Wash light infestations off with a hard spray from the hose aimed into the leaf folds, and a straw mulch on the bed helps hold numbers down. For heavy infestations, ask your local extension office what to use.

pests.name: Onion maggot
pests.identification_seasoned: Wilting, yellowing plants and rotting bulbs riddled by small white larvae; stand loss is worst in cool, wet springs.
pests.identification_beginner: Young plants wilt and yellow, and bulbs rot with small white grubs inside. Worst in cool, wet spring weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the onion maggot fly (Delia antiqua), which lays at the base of the plant; the pupae overwinter in the soil around last season's shallots or onions, and cull piles and volunteer onions keep the fly going between crops. Rotting organic matter and spring manure draw egg-laying, and cool, wet springs favor the maggots.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae (maggots) of a small fly that lays its eggs at the base of onion-family plants. It spends the winter in the soil where onions or shallots grew the year before, and old bulbs and rotting garden waste draw it in.
pests.management_seasoned: Rotate off ground that carried alliums last season and site new plantings away from it, remove culls and volunteer alliums, keep spring manure and green manure out of the bed, and cover the sets with row cover sealed at the edges from planting, before the spring flight, on ground that did not carry alliums last year. Where the season allows, planting after the first flight has passed reduces damage.
pests.management_beginner: Do not plant shallots where onions or their relatives grew last year, clear out old bulbs and any volunteers, keep fresh manure out of the bed in spring, and cover the young plants with row-cover fabric from planting day so the fly cannot lay eggs on them. Do not cover a bed that grew alliums last year, or you seal the emerging flies in with the crop.

pests.name: Allium leafminer
pests.identification_seasoned: Rows of white dots punched down a leaf edge (egg-laying scars), then twisted, distorted leaves; cream-colored larvae mine the leaves and tunnel down into the bulb, where their pupae overwinter.
pests.identification_beginner: Look for a neat line of small white dots along the leaves, then leaves that twist and curl. Tiny pale grubs tunnel inside the leaves and down into the bulb.
pests.cause_seasoned: The allium leafminer (Phytomyza gymnostoma), an invasive fly that attacks alliums including shallot; adults fly and lay eggs in a spring generation (about March into May) and again in fall (September into October).
pests.cause_beginner: A small invasive fly that attacks onions, shallots, garlic, and leeks. The adults come out and lay eggs in spring and again in fall, and the grubs tunnel into the plants.
pests.management_seasoned: Floating row cover or insect netting installed before each flight and sealed at the edges gives close to full control; time it to the spring and fall adult emergence, rotate away from alliums, and use spinosad if covers are not practical.
pests.management_beginner: Cover the plants with row-cover fabric or fine netting before the flies appear in spring and again in fall, sealing the edges so none get in. Rotating where you plant alliums helps too. A spinosad spray is an option if you cannot use covers.

diseases.name: White rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting, dying-back leaves, then a fluffy white mat of mycelium at the base and on the bulb studded with tiny black, poppyseed-like sclerotia; clumps collapse and rot.
diseases.identification_beginner: Leaves turn yellow and wilt, and the base of the plant grows a fluffy white mold dotted with tiny black specks. The bulbs rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne fungus (Sclerotium cepivorum) that attacks only alliums and favors cool, moist soil. Its sclerotia survive in the ground for over 20 years, so once a bed is infested it stays infested.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that attacks only onions, shallots, garlic, and leeks. It likes cool, damp soil, and its survival specks last in the ground for decades, so an infected bed stays a problem for years.
diseases.management_seasoned: There is no rescue once it appears. Avoid introducing it on infested sets or soil, remove and dispose of infected clumps (do not compost), and rotate alliums out of the bed for as long as possible; the disease is essentially permanent in infested ground.
diseases.management_beginner: There is no cure once it shows up, so the goal is to keep it out. Buy clean sets, pull and throw away (do not compost) any infected plants, and do not grow alliums in that spot again for many years.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.identification_seasoned: Pale, elongated patches on the leaves carrying a fuzzy gray-violet sporulation in humid mornings; affected leaves yellow and collapse, cutting bulb size.
diseases.identification_beginner: Pale patches on the leaves with a fuzzy gray-purple coating in damp weather. The leaves yellow and flop, and the bulbs end up smaller.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus-like pathogen Peronospora destructor, favored by cool, wet, humid conditions and lingering leaf wetness; it spreads fast in crowded, poorly aired plantings.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mildew that spreads in cool, wet, humid weather, especially when the leaves stay wet and the plants are crowded.
diseases.management_seasoned: Space for airflow, water at the base to keep foliage dry, and rotate away from alliums for three years or longer where the disease has occurred. Destroy infected debris, cull piles and volunteer alliums, and hold nitrogen back, since an overproduction of succulent leaves promotes it. No resistant variety is available, so every lever here is a growing-conditions one.
diseases.management_beginner: Give the plants room for air to move, water at the base so the leaves stay dry, and rotate where you plant. Clear away sick leaves and pull out any volunteer onions nearby, since they carry the disease over. Go easy on nitrogen, because soft, sappy growth suits it. There is no resistant variety to fall back on, so the growing conditions are the whole of the defense.

diseases.name: Botrytis neck rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: A soft, sunken rot starting at the neck in storage, often with gray mold; immature or poorly cured clumps are most susceptible.
diseases.identification_beginner: Shallots go soft and rotten at the neck after harvest, sometimes with gray mold. It mostly hits bulbs that were not dried well.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis infection of immature or insufficiently cured necks; excess late nitrogen and bent-over green tops worsen it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold that gets into the neck of shallots that were harvested too green or not dried properly. Too much late fertilizer and bending the tops down make it worse.
diseases.management_seasoned: Let tops mature naturally, do not knock down green tops to force bulbing, cure thoroughly until necks are tight, and store cool and dry.
diseases.management_beginner: Let the tops fall on their own, do not bend them over, dry (cure) the shallots well until the necks are tight, and store them somewhere cool and dry.

diseases.name: Pink root
diseases.identification_seasoned: Roots turn pink then red and shrivel, stunting plants and shrinking the clump; common where alliums are grown repeatedly and in warm soils.
diseases.identification_beginner: The roots turn pink, then red, then shrivel up. Plants stay small and make small clumps. Common when alliums are grown in the same place often.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne fungus (Setophoma terrestris, long known as Phoma terrestris) that penetrates the roots directly without a wound and builds up with every onion-family crop on the same ground; it is most active at soil temperatures of 75 to 85°F, and weak or stressed plants in heavy, wet soil are the most susceptible. Shallots are a form of the same species as onion and get it the same way.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that builds up when shallots and their relatives are grown in the same ground year after year. Stressed plants get it worst.
diseases.management_seasoned: Rotate off allium ground for three to six years, understanding that rotation reduces the disease rather than clearing it, because the fungus persists in soil for years. Keep plants vigorous with steady water and fertility, since weak roots are the ones it takes, and improve drainage on heavy ground.
diseases.management_beginner: Give shallots a bed that has not grown onions or their relatives for several years, keep them watered and fed so the roots stay strong, and improve drainage where the soil stays wet. Rotation helps but does not clear the fungus, which lasts in the soil for years.
